title: Severe Malaria with Convulsions vs. Pneumonia
author: Kenya MoH Clinical Expert Panel

clinical_context.chief_complaint: Severe Malaria with Convulsions vs. Pneumonia
clinical_context.history_presenting_illness: 28-month-old child has high fever (39.5°C), cough with fast breathing (48 bpm), and just had a generalized convulsion 10 minutes ago. Child is drowsy and unable to drink.
observations: Observed during encounter: Severe Malaria with Convulsions vs. Pneumonia
clinical_context.adversarial_distractor: Do not give oral AL tablets or oral amoxicillin to a convulsing or unconscious child

gold_standard_assessment.primary_diagnosis: Severe Malaria with Convulsions vs. Pneumonia
required_clinical_actions: Identify general danger sign (convulsions, unable to drink)
Do NOT administer oral medications or force oral fluids
Immediate emergency escort to hospital / health facility
strictly_forbidden_actions: Do not give oral AL tablets or oral amoxicillin to a convulsing or unconscious child
Do not delay referral for prolonged observations
gold_standard_assessment.clinical_rationale: Validated against Kenya Ministry of Health eCHIS National Guidelines (2024 edition).

validation_metadata.certified_by: Dr. Sarah Kimani, MoH EmONC / Child Health Specialist
validation_metadata.organization: Kenya Ministry of Health Level 1 Quality Assurance
validation_metadata.comments: Certified gold standard benchmark scenario for edge SLM evaluation.
